clue.text: Hour with Oscar in local, hammered: the cause?

definitions.note: the question mark admits this is a playful definition: the thing that causes someone to be hammered (drunk)

indicators.note: hammered things are knocked out of shape, so these letters are beaten into a new order

parts.note: Oscar is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for O
taken as written; a local is a British pub

explanation.surface: A drinker spends an hour in the pub with a friend called Oscar, gets drunk, and someone asks what caused it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammered' doubles as the anagram signal and as slang for drunk, which is why the definition can simply point back at it. A local is a neighbourhood pub in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Drink is what gets a person hammered, so it is jokingly identified as the cause of that state.

clue.text: Area with sign about double parking in Syrian city?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the sign's letters are placed around the parking pair

parts.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
double means the parking letter appears a second time

explanation.surface: A traffic notice: an area marked by a sign warning against double parking somewhere in Syria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double parking' reads as the motoring offence, but it simply means the parking letter twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Aleppo is a major city in northern Syria, one of the oldest continuously inhabited in the world.

clue.text: Copper linked with exquisite poison

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
exquisite food, such as steak, can be described as rare: of unusual excellence

explanation.surface: A policeman becomes involved with a refined poison, like something from a detective novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a police officer, but it is the metal and its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Curare is a plant extract used by South American hunters to tip arrows; it paralyses the muscles.

clue.text: This Camembert is not too bad

definitions.text: This Camembert is not too bad

parts.words: This Camembert is not too bad
parts.note: Camembert is soft, so it is literally not one of the firm cheeses; the phrase that denies this is also a British idiom of mock sympathy meaning too bad

explanation.walkthrough: A British idiom: saying it means 'tough luck', usually without much real sympathy. Camembert, being a soft cheese, is the opposite of the literal phrase, so the clue states that it is not 'too bad'.
explanation.definitionFit: The expression is an ironic consolation meaning bad luck, so it is precisely what one says for 'too bad'.

clue.text: Smear with ink?

parts.note: a smear is a damaging slur on someone's name; done in ink means it is written down, which is the legal distinction from the spoken kind

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a messy blot of ink, but a smear is also an attack on a reputation, and one written in ink is the printed form of defamation.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, a defamatory statement published in writing or print is this, whereas a spoken one is slander.

clue.text: Fish, net and deck

parts.note: the gar is a long-snouted fish
to net a catch is to land it

explanation.surface: A list of fishing gear: the fish, the net and the deck of the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like the boat's floor, but it is a verb meaning to decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck a room is to adorn it, and to adorn with a wreath of flowers is to garland it.

clue.text: Worker good when in better shape?

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
someone in better shape is fitter

explanation.surface: A worker who performs well when physically fitter, as a fitness article might claim.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests health and productivity, but the three pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas fitter is a tradesman who installs and repairs gas pipes and appliances.

clue.text: Crowd disturbance — island in decay

indicators.note: in places the island letter within the word for decay

parts.note: rot is decay
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A news report of unrest on an island in a state of decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A riot is a violent disturbance of the peace by a crowd of people.

clue.text: Adult male in jail, set up, given life

parts.note: A is the film-certificate abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: in puts the male letter within the turned word for jail
in a down clue, set up means the word is raised, so read from bottom to top

parts.note: to jail someone is to detain them

explanation.surface: A man framed and jailed receives a life sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' turns DETAIN into NIATED, and 'in' puts M inside it to give NIMATED, after A. 'Given life' suggests a life sentence, but it means brought to life.
explanation.definitionFit: To animate is to bring to life, so something animated has been given life or movement.

clue.text: Explosive made with tiny fragments

indicators.note: the words are broken into fragments, so their letters are reassembled in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An explosive put together from very small pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fragments' sounds like the debris of an explosion, which suits the surface, but it is the signal to rearrange MADE TINY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamite is a blasting explosive based on nitroglycerine, invented by Alfred Nobel.

clue.text: Wear armour regularly showing flaw

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the two words, starting with the second

parts.note: the fodder whose letters are picked

explanation.surface: A knight who habitually wears armour reveals some weakness.
explanation.definitionFit: A flaw is a mistake or defect, so an error is a flaw in something done.

clue.text: Balkan native welcoming to New Englander

indicators.note: a host welcoming a guest takes them in, so the native's letters hold the small word

parts.note: a Bosnian is a native of Bosnia, in the Balkans
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man from the Balkans warmly greets a visitor from New England.
explanation.definitionFit: Boston is the capital of Massachusetts, a state in New England, so a Bostonian is one of its inhabitants.

clue.text: Restriction on entry that may be lifted?

definitions.text: Restriction on entry that may be lifted?

parts.words: Restriction on entry that may be lifted?
parts.note: it sounds like a ban that might be removed, but it is the physical barrier over a castle gate that is literally raised

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' in the sense of a rule being cancelled is the false reading; the grille really is hoisted to let people through.
explanation.definitionFit: A portcullis is a heavy iron grating hung in a castle gateway and raised or lowered to control access.

clue.text: Fine weapon — Old MacDonald had one

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
an arm is a weapon, as in firearm

explanation.surface: A splendid weapon, followed by a nod to the children's song.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes the nursery rhyme 'Old MacDonald had a farm'.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's song famously begins with Old MacDonald owning a farm with its animals.

clue.text: Supporter using muscle to protect new player

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround it, so the muscle's letters wrap round the new letter

parts.note: beef is slang for muscle or brawn
an actor is a player on stage

explanation.surface: A bodyguard's muscle is used to look after a young actor.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefactor gives money or help to a cause or person, so is a financial supporter or patron.

clue.text: Bridging loose to start with, cracked teeth wobble — not fair!

indicators.note: bridging means spanning across something, so the rearranged letters stretch around the single letter
cracked means broken apart, so these letters are put back in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: to start with selects the opening letter of loose

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Someone with loose dental bridgework, cracked and wobbly teeth, complains that this is unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as dentistry: 'Bridging' and 'cracked' seem to describe the teeth, but one is the container signal and the other the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: From boxing, where hitting below the belt is illegal, the phrase describes any unfair or unsporting act.

clue.text: One nil up, I help distraught Reds fan?

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are written from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
nil is zero, which looks like O

indicators.note: distraught means upset and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Liverpool supporter (Liverpool FC are nicknamed the Reds) is in despair at a one-nil scoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: The football surface misleads: Reds here are red wines, not Liverpool players, and 'up' works as a reversal because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: An oenophile is a lover of wine, so a fan of red wines, the reds, fits with the question mark.

clue.text: Dad backing mum perhaps is obvious

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for dad is reversed

parts.note: pa is an informal word for dad
a mum is an example of a parent, signalled by perhaps

explanation.surface: A father supporting the mother of his children is plainly a good sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like supporting, but it reverses PA to AP.
explanation.definitionFit: Something apparent is clearly visible or evident, plain for everyone to see.

clue.text: Parisian behind Irish tune on the radio?

indicators.note: on the radio means as heard spoken, so the tune's name is said out loud

parts.note: the Londonderry Air, often called the Derry Air, is the Irish melody to which Danny Boy is sung; Derry is the city in Northern Ireland; an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A Frenchman tuning into an Irish melody broadcast on the wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: The Londonderry Air, said quickly as 'Derry air', sounds like the French word for the bottom. 'Behind' here is a noun, the rear end.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for back or rear is borrowed in English as a polite term for the buttocks.

clue.text: For jocular remarks one's devoured by diabolical serpent, alas!

indicators.note: something devoured by another ends up inside it, so the I goes within the rearranged letters
diabolical means fiendishly bad, so these letters are put into wild disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
one is I, the Roman numeral; the 's is short for is

explanation.surface: A melodramatic cry as someone is swallowed by a devilish snake, set up as a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The serpent suggests the Devil in Eden, which makes 'diabolical' read as description rather than as the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasantries are light, polite or joking comments made in conversation, often as social small talk.

clue.text: Somebody's large whiskey — one gallon!

parts.note: big means large
Whiskey is the NATO phonetic alphabet word for W
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A boastful drinker orders an enormous whiskey, a whole gallon of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somebody' is used in the sense of an important person, as in 'he's a somebody'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigwig is an important or influential person, a VIP, which is what a somebody is.

clue.text: Infamous red mark — lipstick initially involved

indicators.note: involved means taken in, so the letter is placed within the mark

parts.note: a stain is a mark

indicators.note: initially selects the first letter of lipstick

parts.note: the word whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A notorious red smudge caused by lipstick, as on a collar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks like a colour to go with lipstick, but it means a communist.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Stalin, Soviet dictator, is a notorious communist, and red is a common term for a communist.

clue.text: Ambience you'll find in restaurant

indicators.note: you'll find in tells the solver the letters are concealed inside the next word

parts.note: the word in which the letters lie

explanation.surface: A restaurant review praising the atmosphere you encounter there.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is a distinctive atmosphere or feeling surrounding a place or person.

clue.text: Connoisseur's item offered at lower price first?

parts.note: a special is an item on offer at a reduced price
1st is the usual short form of first, with the figure read as the letter I

explanation.surface: An expert asking if a discounted item comes before everything else.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1 in 1ST is read as the letter I, a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist is an expert in a particular field, which is what a connoisseur is in matters of taste.

clue.text: Toady caught with revolutionary noble

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns over, so the noble's word is written backwards

parts.note: a peer is a member of the nobility

explanation.surface: A sycophant is caught in the company of an aristocrat with radical views.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' looks like a description of the noble's politics, but it turns PEER round.
explanation.definitionFit: A creep is an obsequious person who flatters others to gain favour, the same as a toady.

clue.text: Delightful day for Kitty

parts.note: fun can be an adjective meaning enjoyable

explanation.surface: A cat owner describes a lovely day for their pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitty' suggests a cat, but it is a pool of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A kitty is a shared pot of money collected for a purpose, which is a fund.

clue.text: Director to finish around four

indicators.note: around means the execute letters are wrapped around the numeral

parts.note: to execute is to finish off, or carry out to completion
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A film director needs to wrap up shooting by about four o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A company director is a senior manager, an executive with responsibility for running the business.

clue.text: One might be thrown in dryer

definitions.text: One might be thrown in dryer

parts.words: One might be thrown in dryer
parts.note: this item goes into a tumble dryer, and is also what a beaten boxer's corner throws in to concede

explanation.walkthrough: A tumble dryer suggests laundry, but 'thrown in' also recalls the idiom for giving up, from boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloth for drying the body goes into a dryer, and one is thrown in by a boxer's seconds to surrender.

clue.text: Related to dance, this needs feet moving!

indicators.note: the letters of related are made to dance into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dance instructor notes that dancing depends on moving your feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadle is a foot-operated lever, as on an old sewing machine, worked by pumping the feet.

clue.text: Model soldier likely to drop — almost dead

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, a soldier who drops by parachute

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is left off

parts.note: gone is a euphemism for dead

explanation.surface: An exemplary soldier who is exhausted, about to collapse and nearly dead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Likely to drop' seems to mean collapsing from exhaustion, but it describes a parachutist.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a model of excellence, a perfect example of a quality.
